title: RAG Pipelines

techniques.name: Document Parsing and OCR
techniques.q: Did the text, tables and layout survive ingestion?
techniques.what: Turns PDFs, scans, slides and spreadsheets into clean text with its structure before anything is chunked or embedded. Digital pages give up their text layer; scanned pages need OCR, including Hindi and other Indian scripts; layout detection restores reading order across columns and drops running headers; tables are kept as rows with their headers; and page and section numbers travel with the text for citations. What is lost here cannot be retrieved later.
use: Scanned KYC forms, agreements and old circulars
Reports and statements full of tables
Multi-column documents such as regulations and research papers
metrics: extract digital text directly; it is exact and fast
render scans at about 300 dpi; set the languages, such as eng + hin
Markdown or HTML rows that keep the header
document, page, section and date for citations and filters
empty pages, garbled characters, low OCR confidence
steps: Check each page for a text layer and OCR only the pages without one
Restore reading order and drop running headers and footers
Convert tables to Markdown with their header row
Keep page and section metadata, and send near-empty pages to review
pitfalls: Scanned pages ingested as blank text, silently
Tables flattened into a stream of numbers with no headers
Two-column pages read straight across both columns
techniques.remember: Parse for structure, not just text.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kosh Finance, a fictional NBFC, ingests 2,000 pages of loan files: digital, scanned, tabular and two-column.

techniques.name: Chunking Strategies
techniques.q: Does each retrieved piece hold the whole answer?
techniques.what: Splits parsed documents into the pieces that are embedded and retrieved. Size and boundaries decide whether a retrieved chunk contains the full answer: too small and a rule loses its exception, too large and the embedding blurs and the prompt fills with noise. Common strategies are fixed-size with overlap, recursive splitting by paragraph and sentence, structure-aware splitting by heading or clause, semantic splitting where the topic shifts, and small-to-big retrieval that searches small chunks but returns their parent section.
use: Long, structured documents: policies, contracts, manuals, regulations
Answers that depend on a condition or exception
Corpora where a few chunk types answer most questions
metrics: simple baseline; cuts through sentences and clauses
split on paragraphs, then sentences, until under the size
split on headings, clauses or slides
split where the embedding similarity drops
search small chunks, return the parent section
prepend the title and section path to each chunk
steps: Split by the document’s own structure, then recursively to about 300–500 tokens
Overlap by 10–15% so sentences at a boundary appear in both chunks
Prepend the document title and section path to every chunk
Evaluate recall on real questions for each strategy before choosing
pitfalls: Tiny chunks that separate a rule from its exception
Huge chunks that waste context and dilute the embedding
Every change of chunking means re-embedding the whole corpus
techniques.remember: Cut along the document’s structure and carry its context.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Pragati Insurance, a fictional insurer, answers 120 questions about its policy wordings.

techniques.name: Query Rewriting and HyDE
techniques.q: Can a model turn the question into a better search?
techniques.what: Uses an LLM before retrieval to make the question searchable. It rewrites a chatty follow-up into a standalone query using the conversation, generates a few alternative phrasings and fuses their results (multi-query), splits a multi-part question into sub-queries, or writes a hypothetical answer and embeds that instead of the question (HyDE). Each trick raises recall at the cost of an LLM call. Ordering the results afterwards is a separate step: re-ranking.
use: Conversational follow-ups such as “and the other one?”
Documents that use different words from the users
Multi-part questions that need several searches
metrics: turn chatty or vague input into a standalone search query
search several phrasings and merge with reciprocal rank fusion
embed a hypothetical answer instead of the question
split a complex question into sub-queries
search a more general question alongside the specific one
steps: Rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries using the chat history
Add multi-query with fusion when documents use varied wording
Try HyDE for short or vague questions and compare with the plain query
Measure recall and latency before and after each addition
pitfalls: Every LLM step adds latency and cost
Rewrites can drift from what the user meant
HyDE can invent details that pull retrieval off course
techniques.remember: Fix the question before you search.
techniques.cap: Rewriting puts the right passage in the pool; re-ranking then moves it up.

techniques.name: Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders
techniques.q: Are the best passages at the top, not just somewhere in the pool?
techniques.what: A second stage after retrieval. Fast search, dense or hybrid, fetches a wide candidate set such as the top 50; a cross-encoder then reads the query and each candidate together and scores how well the passage answers it, and only the top few reach the prompt. Reading both texts together is far more precise than comparing two separate vectors, but it costs time per candidate, and it can only reorder what the first stage found.
use: Help centres and knowledge bases where the top 3 to 5 decide the answer
Hindi, Hinglish and mixed-language queries (with a multilingual model)
Pipelines that must say “not found” instead of guessing
metrics: how many first-stage results to score, often 30–100
how many reach the prompt, often 3–8
cross-encoder, multilingual cross-encoder or LLM re-ranker
grows with candidates and passage length
drop weak passages so the system can decline
ColBERT-style models sit between bi- and cross-encoders
steps: Retrieve a wide candidate set with hybrid search
Score every candidate with a cross-encoder, multilingual if users mix languages
Keep the top 3 to 8 above a score threshold
Measure recall at the kept depth and p95 latency together
pitfalls: Re-ranking cannot rescue a passage the first stage never retrieved
English-only re-rankers hurt Hindi and Hinglish queries
Scores are not calibrated probabilities; tune the threshold on your data
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Vyapar Mart, a fictional marketplace, answers seller questions from 8,000 help articles.

techniques.name: Citations and Grounded Answers
techniques.q: Can every sentence in the answer be traced to a source?
techniques.what: Makes answers checkable. The model answers only from the retrieved passages and cites a source for each claim; the system checks that the cited text really is in that source and supports the sentence, drops what is unsupported, and says “not found” when nothing supports an answer. Sources are shown with the document, section, page and effective date, and superseded versions are filtered out before the model sees them.
use: Policy, HR, legal and compliance assistants
Customer-facing answers about fees, limits and eligibility
Any answer a person will act on or an auditor may question
metrics: each passage labelled with title, section and date
a source after every sentence, not one list at the end
the exact span the claim rests on
the span exists in the source and supports the claim
steps: Label each passage with its title, section and effective date, and filter out superseded versions
Instruct the model to answer only from the sources and cite each sentence
Verify every citation in code and drop sentences that fail
Say “not found” when nothing is supported, and show the sources
pitfalls: Citations that point to a real passage that does not say what the sentence claims
Valid citations to an outdated version of a policy
Forcing an answer when the sources are empty
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, runs a staff policy assistant with 100 test questions.

techniques.name: Agentic and Corrective RAG
techniques.q: Should the agent plan, check and retry its own retrieval?
techniques.what: An agent plans retrieval instead of running one fixed search. It pulls structured filters out of the question, chooses the collection or tool, and checks what came back. Corrective RAG (CRAG) adds a grader that scores the retrieved passages: weak results trigger a rewritten query, a different source such as web search, or an honest “not found”. Self-querying retrieval is the filter-extraction part of this pattern.
use: Questions with implicit filters: dates, prices, categories, owners
Several collections or data sources to choose between
Hard questions where a first search often misses
metrics: “laptops under ₹60k from 2024” → price and year filters
which collection, index or tool to query
a small model scores each passage: relevant, ambiguous or wrong
rewrite, switch source or abstain when grades are low
top-k, filters and a cap on retries
steps: Have the agent output a structured query plan that code validates
Grade the retrieved passages before generating
Rewrite, switch source or abstain when grades are low, with a hard cap on retries
Log every plan and grade, and compare against a fixed pipeline on your eval set
pitfalls: Adds LLM calls and latency before every answer
A wrong filter silently excludes the right results
Unbounded retry loops; always cap them
techniques.remember: Plan the query, grade the results, retry or admit defeat.
techniques.cap: The plan is plain JSON, so code can validate filters before anything runs.

cmp.needs: Implicit filters, many sources, hard questions

techniques.name: GraphRAG
techniques.q: Can retrieval answer questions about the whole corpus?
techniques.what: GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from the documents before any question arrives. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from every chunk, a clustering algorithm (Leiden) groups them into communities, and the LLM writes a summary of each community. Local search starts from entities named in the question and gathers their neighbours and source chunks, which helps multi-hop questions. Global search combines community summaries in a map-reduce step to answer questions about the whole corpus, such as the main themes, which vector search over single chunks answers poorly. Indexing costs far more than embedding, so many teams route only multi-hop and whole-corpus questions to the graph. This is corpus retrieval; a temporal graph of what an agent learns about users is Graph Memory in module 9.
use: Whole-corpus questions: themes, trends, “what are the main issues”
Multi-hop questions that join facts across documents
Investigations over reports, complaints or case files
metrics: LLM pass over every chunk: entities, relationships, claims; the main indexing cost
Leiden clustering at several levels, each with an LLM-written summary
entities in the question → neighbours, relationships and source text
map over community summaries, reduce into one answer
defer summarisation to query time to cut indexing cost
send fact questions to vector RAG and only multi-hop or global ones to the graph
steps: Collect the questions vector RAG fails: multi-hop and whole-corpus
Index a sample with GraphRAG and inspect extracted entities for quality
Route: facts to vector search, multi-hop to local, themes to global
Compare answer quality and cost per 1,000 queries against vector RAG
pitfalls: Indexing the full corpus before checking extraction quality on a sample
Sending every question to global search and paying map-reduce costs for simple facts
Letting the graph go stale when documents change, with no incremental update
techniques.remember: Extract, cluster, summarise; route only the hard questions to the graph.

import fitz                        # PyMuPDF
import pytesseract
from PIL import Image

def page_text(page):
    if len(page.get_text().strip()) >= 50:            # has a text layer   #@1
        h, w = page.rect.height, page.rect.width
        blocks = page.get_text("blocks")              # x0, y0, x1, y1, text, ...   #@3
        body = [b for b in blocks if 50 < b[1] < h - 50]   # drop header, footer   #@3
        body.sort(key=lambda b: (b[0] > w / 2, b[1]))      # left column first   #@3
        return "\n".join(b[4] for b in body), "text"                         #@1,3
    pix = page.get_pixmap(dpi=300)                    # a scan: render it   #@2
    img = Image.frombytes("RGB", (pix.width, pix.height), pix.samples)       #@2
    return pytesseract.image_to_string(img, lang="eng+hin"), "ocr"          #@2

def parse(path, doc_id):
    out = []
    for pno, page in enumerate(fitz.open(path), start=1):
        text, how = page_text(page)
        for t in page.find_tables().tables:           # keep tables as rows   #@4
            out.append({"doc": doc_id, "page": pno, "kind": "table",         #@4,5
                        "text": t.to_markdown()})                            #@4
        out.append({"doc": doc_id, "page": pno, "kind": how, "text": text})  #@5
        if len(text.strip()) < 200:                   # suspiciously empty  #@6
            review_queue.put((doc_id, pno, how))                             #@6
    return out
steps: Check for a text layer
Digital PDFs carry their text; extracting it is exact and takes milliseconds. A page with almost no extractable text is almost certainly a scan.
OCR the scans, in the right languages
Render the scanned page at 300 dpi and run OCR with English and Hindi models. Without “hin”, a Hindi KYC declaration comes back as noise.
Restore the layout
Drop the running header and footer bands, then read the left column before the right. Read straight across, a two-column circular mixes two paragraphs line by line.
Keep tables as tables
The interest-rate table becomes Markdown rows with a header: | Tenure | Rate |. Flattened, it is a stream of numbers no one can match to a question.
Carry the metadata
Every piece keeps its document, page and kind. Citations and filters later depend on it: “loan_2023.pdf, page 7”.
Flag near-empty pages
A page with under 200 characters goes to a review queue. Silent blanks are the most common ingestion bug.

                                      RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter)

headers = [("#", "doc"), ("##", "section"), ("###", "clause")]           #@1
clauses = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(headers_to_split_on=headers)       #@1
sections = clauses.split_text(policy_md)          # one piece per clause  #@1

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_tiktoken_encoder(        #@2
    encoding_name="cl100k_base", chunk_size=400, chunk_overlap=50,       #@2,3
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " "])                                 #@2
chunks = splitter.split_documents(sections)                              #@2

for c in chunks:
    path = " > ".join(c.metadata.get(k, "") for k in ("doc", "section", "clause"))   #@4
    c.page_content = f"[{path}]\n{c.page_content}"                       #@4
    c.metadata["parent"] = path            # the whole clause           #@5
store.add_documents(chunks)

hits = store.similarity_search(question, k=8)                            #@5
context = list(dict.fromkeys(clause_text[h.metadata["parent"]] for h in hits))[:3]   #@5

    print(name, recall_at_k(cfg, eval_questions, k=5), tokens_per_answer(cfg))   #@6
steps: Split along the document’s own structure
Policy wordings are written as sections and clauses. Split on those headings first, so a clause starts and ends where its author meant.
Split long clauses recursively
A clause longer than about 400 tokens is split on paragraphs, then lines, then sentences, never mid-word. Most clauses stay whole.
Overlap the edges
50 tokens of overlap mean a sentence cut at a boundary appears in both neighbours, so “except after 36 months” is not orphaned.
Prepend the section path
“[Policy › Exclusions › 4.2]” goes at the top of the chunk. A question about exclusions now matches a chunk whose text never uses that word.
Search small, return the clause
The search matches small, precise chunks; the prompt receives the whole parent clause, deduplicated, so the rule and its exception arrive together.
Measure each strategy
Compare recall at 5 and tokens per answer on real questions. Any change of chunking means re-embedding the corpus, so decide on evidence.

history  = "User asked about the exit load on the Flexi Cap Fund."
followup = "and what about the other one, the balanced fund?"

query = llm("Rewrite as one standalone search query.\n"          #@1
            f"Chat so far: {history}\nQuestion: {followup}")      #@1
# -> "exit load Balanced Advantage Fund"

variants = llm(f"Give 3 different search phrasings of: {query}").splitlines()   #@2

pools = [hybrid_search(v, k=50) for v in [query, *variants]]   #@3
candidates = rrf(pools)[:50]                                   #@3

reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")   #@4
scores = reranker.predict([(query, c.text) for c in candidates])  #@4
ranked = [c for _, c in sorted(zip(scores, candidates), key=lambda x: -x[0])]   #@4

context = ranked[:5]                                           #@5
answer = llm(prompt(question=query, context=context))          #@5

for name, pipeline in [("baseline", base), ("rewrite+rerank", full)]:   #@6
    r5 = recall_at_k(pipeline, eval_set, k=5)                  #@6

steps: Rewrite the follow-up
“and what about the other one?” has nothing to search on. An LLM uses the chat history to write a standalone query.
Generate alternative phrasings
Multi-query asks for a few rephrasings, because documents may use different words: exit load, redemption charge, exit fee.
Retrieve wide and merge
Run hybrid search for every phrasing, merge the lists with reciprocal rank fusion and keep 50 candidates. The right passage is in the pool, at rank 23.
Re-rank with a cross-encoder
A cross-encoder reads the query and each passage together, which is more accurate than comparing two vectors. The right passage moves from 23 to 2.
Send only the top 5 to the model
Only the best few passages go into the prompt, so the model sees the right one without a pile of noise.
Measure what each step buys
Compare recall@5 and latency with and without each step. Here recall@5 rises from 0.62 to 0.88 for about 410 ms more per query.

reranker = CrossEncoder("BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3", max_length=512)    # multilingual   #@3

def retrieve(query, k_in=50, k_out=5, min_score=0.20):
    candidates = hybrid_search(query, k=k_in)          # cheap and wide: ~40 ms   #@1
    pairs = [(query, c.text) for c in candidates]                       #@2,3
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs, batch_size=32)    # ~2.5 ms a pair on a GPU  #@3
    ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates), key=lambda x: -x[0])       #@4
    kept = [c for s, c in ranked[:k_out] if s >= min_score]             #@5
    return kept or None               # None → say "I could not find this"   #@5

for k_in in (20, 50, 100):                                              #@6

See why the first stage misses
A bi-encoder embeds the query and each article separately and compares two vectors. The article titled “Tax documents for sellers” never shares the question’s words.
Read query and passage together
A cross-encoder scores each (query, passage) pair jointly, attending across both texts. A multilingual model such as bge-reranker-v2-m3 handles the Hinglish.
Sort by the new score
The right article scores 0.94 and moves from rank 17 to rank 1. Articles that merely share words drop.
Keep the few, above a threshold
Only the top 5 with a score of at least 0.20 reach the prompt. If none qualify, the bot says it could not find the answer instead of guessing.

Recall at 5 rises from 0.64 to 0.86 for about 110 ms more at 50 candidates. Deeper pools add recall slowly and latency linearly.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

current = [p for p in passages if p.is_current]        # drop superseded   #@1
docs = [{"type": "document",                                               #@1,2
         "source": {"type": "text", "media_type": "text/plain", "data": p.text},   #@1
         "title": f"{p.title} §{p.section} · effective {p.effective}",   #@1
         "citations": {"enabled": True}} for p in current]                #@2

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=800,
    system="Answer only from the documents. If they do not answer, say so.",   #@2,5
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": docs + [{"type": "text", "text": question}]}])

answer, sources = [], []
for block in msg.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    cites = block.citations or []                                          #@3
    ok = [c for c in cites if c.cited_text in current[c.document_index].text]   #@4
    if states_a_fact(block.text) and not ok:                               #@4
        continue                            # unsupported: drop the sentence   #@4
    answer.append(block.text)
    sources += [(c.document_title, c.cited_text) for c in ok]              #@6
reply = "".join(answer) if sources else "I could not find this in the policies."   #@5,6
steps: Label the sources, current versions only
Each passage becomes a document with its title, section and effective date. The 2023 leave policy is superseded, so it is filtered out before the model sees it.
Switch on citations and ground the prompt
With citations enabled, the model’s answer comes back as text blocks, each carrying the source spans it relied on. The system prompt says: answer only from the documents.
Read what each sentence rests on
Every citation names the document and quotes the exact cited text, for example “10 working days of paternity leave”.
Verify in code, drop what fails
Check that each cited span is really in that document. A sentence that states a fact without a valid citation is dropped, not shown.
No support, no answer
If nothing survives verification, the assistant says it could not find the answer. Declining beats a confident guess about someone’s leave.

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
BRANDS = {"Acer", "Apple", "Asus", "Dell", "HP", "Lenovo"}           #@1

class Plan(BaseModel):                                              #@1
    query: str                               # the semantic part     #@1
    max_price_inr: int | None = Field(None, ge=10_000)              #@1,3
    year: int | None = Field(None, ge=2018, le=2026)                #@1,3
    brand: str | None = None                                        #@1
    mode: Literal["hybrid", "vector", "keyword"] = "hybrid"         #@1
    k: int = Field(10, le=50)                                       #@1

    @field_validator("brand")                                       #@3
    @classmethod                                                    #@3
    def known_brand(cls, v):                                        #@3
        if v is not None and v not in BRANDS:                       #@3
            raise ValueError(f"unknown brand: {v}")                 #@3
        return v                                                    #@3

def make_plan(request, note=""):                                    #@2
    msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": f"Fill the search plan. Today is 2026-09-25. {note}"},   #@2
            {"role": "user", "content": request}]                   #@2
    return client.beta.chat.completions.parse(model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=msgs,   #@2
                                              response_format=Plan).choices[0].message.parsed   #@2

request = "2024 laptops under 60k with long battery life"
plan = make_plan(request)             # an invalid plan raises ValidationError: ask again   #@2,3
for attempt in range(2):              # hard cap on retries   #@5
    hits = db.search(plan.query, mode=plan.mode, k=plan.k,          #@4
                     where={"price_inr": ("<", plan.max_price_inr), "year": ("=", plan.year)})   #@4
    log.info({"request": request, "plan": plan.model_dump(), "hits": len(hits)})   #@6
    if len(hits) >= 3: break                                        #@5
    plan = make_plan(request, note=f"Only {len(hits)} results. Relax the least important filter.")   #@5

A typed plan lists the fields the database can filter on, with ranges and allowed values. The model can only fill these fields.

The request becomes a semantic query plus structured filters: year 2024 and a price ceiling. Here the model slips and writes 60.
Validate the plan in code
ge=10_000 rejects a price of 60 before any search runs. The error goes back to the model, which returns 60,000.
Run the structured search
Filters are applied exactly by the database; only the “long battery life” part is matched by meaning.
Check the results, retry once
Fewer than 3 hits triggers one re-plan with feedback. The loop is capped so a bad request can't spin forever.

steps: Set up a project

Sahayak Telecom, a fictional operator, puts 5,000 outage and complaint reports into a GraphRAG project. The settings choose the chat and embedding models and the entity types: tower, vendor, circle, fault.
Extract the graph
Indexing sends every chunk to the LLM to pull out entities and relationships. This is the costly step, about ₹18,000 for this corpus, so it is tried on a 200-report sample first.
Cluster and summarise
Leiden clustering groups related entities into communities at several levels, and the LLM writes a report for each: “Pune circle, vendor X, repeated power faults”.
Route by question type
A small classifier sends simple fact questions to vector RAG, which is cheaper and just as good for them.
Local or global
Multi-hop questions go to local search, which walks entity neighbours. Whole-corpus questions go to global search, which maps over community reports and reduces the partial answers.
Measure
On 300 test questions, 30% of them about themes, vector RAG alone scores 59%; the routed setup scores 82%, at about ₹1,370 per 1,000 queries.

chunk.title: Adding the section path
chunk.code:
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_tiktoken_encoder(
    encoding_name="cl100k_base", chunk_size=400, chunk_overlap=50)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(sections)
for c in chunks:
    path = " > ".join(c.metadata.get(k, "") for k in ("doc", "section", "clause"))
    c.metadata["path"] = path
store.add_documents(chunks)
chunk.explain: The path is stored only as metadata, which is not embedded, so a question that names the section still has nothing to match in the chunk text. Prepend it to the content that gets embedded.

also.2: A 50-token overlap on 400-token chunks is a sensible default.
also.3: Splitting the clause-level sections keeps chunk boundaries inside clauses.

rerank.title: Re-ranking the candidates
rerank.code:
def retrieve(query, k_in=50, k_out=5):
    candidates = hybrid_search(query, k=k_out)
    pairs = [(query, c.text) for c in candidates]
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs)
    ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates), key=lambda x: -x[0])
    return [c for _, c in ranked[:k_out]]
rerank.explain: The first stage fetches only k_out = 5 candidates, so the re-ranker merely reshuffles the same five. The point of re-ranking is to score a wide pool and keep a few.

also.4: Scoring (query, passage) pairs is exactly how a cross-encoder is used.
also.5: Sorting by descending score is correct.

cite.title: Verifying citations
cite.explain: This checks that the cited text appears in the answer, which proves nothing. The check must be against the source document the citation points to.

also.5: Citations can be empty, so the `or []` guard is right.

llm.title: Retrieve, then re-rank
llm.code:
query = rewrite_with_history(history, followup)
candidates = hybrid_search(query, k=5)
scores = reranker.predict([(query, c.text) for c in candidates])
ranked = [c for _, c in sorted(zip(scores, candidates), key=lambda x: -x[0])]
context = ranked[:5]
llm.explain: Retrieving only 5 candidates and keeping 5 means re-ranking can only reorder passages that were already going into the prompt. It can’t add one that sat at rank 23. Retrieve wide, such as 50, then re-rank and keep the top 5.

also.5: Keeping the top 5 after re-ranking is correct. The problem is how few candidates there were to choose from.

qoa.title: Asking a model for a search plan
qoa.code:
class Plan(BaseModel):
    query: str
    max_price_inr: int | None = Field(None, ge=10_000)
    year: int | None = Field(None, ge=2018, le=2026)
msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": "Fill the search plan from the request."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "gaming laptops launched this year"}]
plan = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=msgs, response_format=Plan)
qoa.explain: The model is never told today’s date, so it resolves “this year” from its training data, often a year or two in the past. The result passes validation because 2024 is inside the allowed range, returns plenty of hits, and is silently wrong. Put the current date in the system prompt.
qoa.fix: msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": f"Fill the search plan from the request. Today is {date.today():%Y-%m-%d}."},

also.3: ge=10_000 rejects unit slips such as 60 for “60k”. This is good validation.
also.4: The range is fine. Validation can only reject impossible values, not plausible wrong ones, which is why the date must come from the prompt.

graphrag.title: Routing questions to GraphRAG
graphrag.explain: Multi-hop questions such as “which vendors are linked to Pune outages” need local search over entity neighbours. Sending them to global search pays for a map-reduce over every community report and gives a vaguer answer.

also.2: Sending simple facts to vector RAG is right: it is cheapest for them.
also.5: The query call is fine once the method is right.
