cite: The model answers only from the sources.
Citations are verified against the source.
Old versions are filtered and sources shown.
llm: An LLM helps before and after the search.
It turns vague or follow-up input into a good search query.
Other pre-search tricks: hypothetical answers and sub-queries.
Retrieve many candidates, keep the best few.
Every LLM step adds time and money.
qoa: an agent or LLM plans the search
An LLM plans the retrieval before it runs.
It turns implicit constraints into exact filters.
rewriting or choosing source and strategy
It rewrites the query and chooses the collection, mode and parameters.
A typed plan is validated in code before anything runs.
It grades the results and retries a limited number of times.
cost, latency or silent wrong filters
It adds latency, and a wrong filter can silently hide results, so log every plan.
graphrag: An LLM extracts entities and relationships.
Indexing is costly, so route questions.

parse: A loan PDF page returns 8 characters from its text layer. What is the most likely explanation?
The page is a scanned image and needs OCR
Scanned pages have no real text layer; a stamp or page number may be all that is extractable. Route such pages to OCR.
Claim forms arrive as phone photos in Hindi and English. Which OCR setting matters most?
Both languages enabled, for example eng+hin
Lower image resolution to save time
OCR only recognises scripts it has models for; without Hindi the Devanagari text becomes noise.
A rate table is extracted as “12 m 11.5% 24 m 12.0% 36 m 12.5%”. What is lost?
Which value belongs to which column header
Flattened tables lose their structure; keep them as rows with headers.
Which steps belong in a parsing pipeline for mixed PDFs? Select all that apply.
Detect pages without a text layer
Restore reading order on multi-column pages
Translate every page into English before indexing
Detection, OCR and layout are core. Translation is a separate choice and can hurt exact matching.
A two-column judgment is read straight across each line. What happens to retrieval?
It improves, because lines are longer
Sentences from both columns interleave, so chunks lose their meaning
Interleaved columns produce incoherent text that neither embeddings nor keywords handle well.
500 pages need OCR at 1.5 seconds a page on 4 parallel workers. How long does OCR take?
500 × 1.5 = 750 s of work; ÷ 4 workers ≈ 188 s, about 3 minutes.
Every chunk begins with “Vendor Terms · Confidential · Page n”. What is the effect?
Unrelated chunks look similar, adding noise to retrieval
Running headers repeat on every page and pull unrelated chunks together. Drop them during parsing.
Why keep the page number and section with each parsed piece?
So answers can cite the page and filters can use the section
Metadata enables citations, filters and debugging; it is not mainly for retrieval scores.
After parsing, 60 of 2,000 pages have under 200 characters. What should happen?
Review them: they may be failed OCR, photos or the wrong language
Near-empty pages are the most common silent ingestion failure.
Which tools can OCR or analyse the layout of scanned documents? Select all that apply.
BM25 is a ranking function, not a parser.
A contract PDF is digital, with tables. What is the cheapest correct approach?
Extract the text layer and use a table extractor
Screenshot each page for a vision model
Digital pages already carry exact text; OCR would only add errors and time.
Why is OCR rendered at about 300 dpi rather than 72 dpi?
Small characters need enough pixels to be recognised
Low resolution blurs small text; 300 dpi is a common default for OCR.
A scheme notice mixes Hindi and English on the same page. What is the best OCR setup?
OCR twice and keep the longer output
Mixed-language pages need both models at once.
Parsing changed, so tables are now extracted properly. What else must happen?
Re-chunk and re-embed the affected documents
New text means new chunks and new embeddings.
Test questions answered from tables fail at 65%, others at 10%. What should you inspect first?
How tables were parsed and chunked
The failure concentrates on one page type, which points to parsing.
Which are signs of a parsing problem rather than a retrieval problem? Select all that apply.
The answer text does not appear anywhere in the index
Tables appear as streams of numbers
The right chunk exists but ranks 20th
Two columns interleave in the chunk text
A chunk ranked 20th exists; that is a ranking problem.
A vision-language model can read page images directly. When is that worth it?
For complex visual pages such as charts or forms, where text extraction fails
Vision models are slower and costlier; use them where structure defeats ordinary parsing.
Headers are dropped by removing text in the top and bottom 50 points of each page. What is the risk?
A real heading or table near the edge may be lost; check on samples
Band-based rules are simple; verify them on real layouts.
What is the most useful measure of ingestion quality?
How many test questions have their answer text present in the index
Tie ingestion quality to answerable questions, not raw volume.
A scanned gazette page OCRs with many garbled characters. What could help?
A cleaner scan or preprocessing such as deskewing and binarisation
Image quality drives OCR quality; fix the input before the downstream steps.
chunk: A clause says “pre-existing diseases are excluded” and, 700 tokens later, “except after 36 months”. With 400-token fixed chunks, what happens?
Both sentences are always retrieved together
The exception may be in another chunk and missed
Fixed cuts can separate a rule from its exception.
What does a recursive character splitter do?
Splits at a fixed character count
Tries paragraphs, then lines, then sentences, then words, until pieces fit
It uses the largest natural separator that keeps pieces under the size.
A 1.2 million-token corpus is chunked at 400 tokens with 15% overlap. About how many chunks?
Why prepend “[Policy › Exclusions › 4.2]” to a chunk?
It is required by vector databases
The section path becomes part of the embedded text, so section-level questions match
Chunks often never repeat their section name; the path supplies it.
Searching small chunks but sending their parent section to the model
Using a small model then a big one
Which are symptoms of chunks that are too large? Select all that apply.
Short facts rank lower because the embedding is diluted
Losing exceptions is a symptom of chunks that are too small or badly cut.
k = 5 chunks of 512 tokens reach the prompt. How many tokens is that?
You change chunk size from 512 to 256 tokens in production. What must happen?
Only new documents use the new size
Chunks are the embedded unit; changing them means re-embedding.
a fixed number of tokens is reached
the embedding similarity between neighbouring sentences drops
It places boundaries at topic shifts.
Which should never be split across chunks? Select all that apply.
Rows, code blocks and sentences lose meaning when cut; long documents must be split.
Search returns three small chunks from the same clause. What should reach the prompt with small-to-big?
All three chunks and the clause
Deduplicate parents to keep prompts lean.
Which strategy suits a transcript with no headings?
Without structure to follow, split by meaning or by natural separators.
Recall is 90% at 256-token chunks with small-to-big, using 2,100 tokens per answer. At 512 tokens without it, recall is 88% for 2,560 tokens. Which is better?
256 with small-to-big: higher recall, fewer tokens
So sentences at a boundary appear whole in at least one chunk
Overlap costs a little storage and prevents orphaned sentences.
Product cards are 80 tokens each. How should they be chunked?
Keep each card whole as one chunk
Short, self-contained items are natural chunks.
What should you compare when choosing a chunking strategy? Select all that apply.
Recall at k on real questions
Number of chunks and re-embedding cost
The number of headings in the documents
Measure outcomes and costs; heading counts are an input, not a result.
Anthropic’s contextual retrieval adds what to each chunk before embedding?
A short model-written note situating the chunk in its document
The context note helps chunks match questions phrased in the document’s terms.
At 128-token chunks, questions about rules with exceptions get 40% recall. What is the best fix?
The whole clause must reach the model.
A 900,000-token corpus is chunked at 300 tokens with no overlap. How many chunks?
A guideline’s dosage table is split between two chunks mid-row. What should the chunker do?
Keep table rows intact, splitting only between rows
Split tables only at row boundaries and repeat the header.
rerank: What does a cross-encoder do that a bi-encoder does not?
Reads the query and a passage together to score relevance
Joint reading gives more precise relevance, at more cost per pair.
Recall at 50 is 92% and recall at 5 is 58%. What will help most?
The right passage is usually retrieved but ranked too low: a re-ranking problem.
Recall at 50 is 45%. Will a re-ranker fix it?
No: it can only reorder what was retrieved; fix retrieval first
Re-ranking cannot add passages to the pool.
Search takes 40 ms and re-ranking 2.5 ms per candidate. What is total latency for 100 candidates?
Users write in Hinglish. Which re-ranker?
A multilingual cross-encoder such as bge-reranker-v2-m3
English-only models score code-mixed queries poorly.
Which are reasons to use a score threshold after re-ranking? Select all that apply.
Let the system say “not found” when nothing is relevant
Avoid sending weak passages to the model
Reduce hallucinated answers on unanswerable questions
Make scores comparable across all corpora
Scores are not universally calibrated; tune the threshold per corpus.
Why not run a cross-encoder over the whole corpus?
It must score every query–document pair at query time, which is far too slow
An LLM re-ranker takes 900 ms plus 8 ms per candidate. For 100 candidates, what is its latency?
900 + 100 × 8 = 1,700 ms, too slow for most live chat.
Where does ColBERT-style late interaction sit?
Between bi-encoders and cross-encoders in precision and cost
Token-level matching with precomputed document embeddings.
Which should you measure when tuning candidate depth? Select all that apply.
The number of GPUs in the data centre
Quality and latency together, sliced by segment.
A re-ranker keeps the top 5 of 5 candidates. What is wrong?
It reorders the same 5 it would keep anyway; retrieve a wider pool
Score a wide pool, keep a few.
Re-ranking 200 candidates takes 540 ms against a 500 ms budget. What do you try first?
Score about 100 candidates and check recall
Recall usually changes little between 100 and 200, while latency doubles.
Cross-encoder scores for two different queries are 0.4 and 0.9. What can you conclude?
The second answer is more than twice as likely to be right
Little: scores rank passages within a query, not across queries
The first query should be dropped
Nothing is relevant for the first query
Treat scores as rankings; tune thresholds on labelled data.
Which input format does a cross-encoder take?
It scores one pair at a time, batched for speed.
After adding a re-ranker, answers improve but costs rise because the prompt still carries 20 passages. What should change?
Keep only the top 3 to 8 after re-ranking
The point of re-ranking is to send fewer, better passages.
Which are hosted or open re-rankers? Select all that apply.
HNSW is an index, not a re-ranker.
Recall at 5 rises from 64% to 86% with re-ranking. How many more of 500 questions have the right passage in the top 5?
Why might a re-ranker hurt some queries?
A domain or language mismatch can push good passages down; evaluate per segment
Measure by segment, not just overall.
Long passages are truncated at 512 tokens by the re-ranker. What is the risk?
The relevant sentence may be beyond the cut, so the passage scores low
Keep chunks within the re-ranker’s window, or use a long-context re-ranker.
Did we retrieve the right passage at all?
Are the best passages at the top of what we retrieved?
cite: What does “grounded” mean for a RAG answer?
Every claim is supported by the provided sources
Groundedness is support by sources, not style.
A citation points to a real policy passage, but the passage does not say what the sentence claims. What catches this?
Checking that the cited span supports the claim, for figures that the number appears in it
Existence of a citation is not support; verify the content.
All citations verify, yet answers quote a 2023 policy replaced in 2025. What is missing?
Version filtering by effective date or a current flag
Valid citations to outdated sources pass verification; filter versions before retrieval.
Which belong in a grounded-answer pipeline? Select all that apply.
Let the model add facts it is confident about
Model knowledge without a source breaks grounding.
Nothing in the sources answers the question. What should the assistant do?
Say it could not find the answer in the documents
Pick the closest passage and answer
Abstaining beats a confident wrong answer.
Staff take 90 seconds to check an answer without citations and 15 seconds with a source per sentence. For 400 answers a day, how many staff-hours are saved?
Why cite after each sentence rather than listing sources at the end?
Each claim can be traced and checked on its own
Claim-level citations make checking fast and specific.
With Anthropic’s Citations feature, what comes back with the answer?
Only a list of document titles
Text blocks carrying the exact cited text and the document it came from
The cited spans are what you verify.
Which metadata should each source carry for display? Select all that apply.
People need to find and trust the source; vectors mean nothing to them.
Verification removes 80% of unsupported claims. If 6 answers of 80 have one before verification, how many remain?
Adding an abstain rule costs 3 answerable questions but declines 7 more unanswerable ones. Is it worth it?
Usually, where wrong answers are costly; measure both numbers
It depends on the model size
Weigh false abstentions against confident wrong answers for your use.
What does the Ragas faithfulness metric measure?
How many claims in the answer are supported by the retrieved context
Where should superseded versions be filtered?
Before retrieval, as a metadata filter
In the prompt, by asking the model to ignore them
Filter before the model sees them; prompts are not a reliable filter.
A citizen assistant must show where each rule comes from. What is the minimum?
A link to the ministry home page
The document, section and date for each cited claim
Which are warning signs of weak grounding? Select all that apply.
Citations whose text is not in the source
Numbers in the answer that do not appear in the cited span
Length is not a grounding signal.
The model cites passage 3 for “the fee is ₹500”, but passage 3 says ₹250. What should verification do?
Reject the sentence because the figure is not in the cited text
For figures, check the number itself appears in the cited span.
A free prompt yields 18% answers with unsupported claims; a grounded prompt yields 9%. What does grounding alone not guarantee?
That the remaining claims are supported; verification is still needed
Prompts reduce the rate; code checks enforce it.
Why is “not found” sometimes the best answer?
When sources do not support an answer, any answer would be a guess
In code, after generation and before display
Deterministic checks after generation, before anyone sees the answer.
What does citation verification not catch?
A cited span missing from the source
A correct citation to an outdated document
A number that differs from the cited text
The span is real; the document is stale. Use version filtering.
llm: Mid-chat, “what about the second one?” retrieves unrelated documents. What is the fix?
Rewrite the query with an LLM using the chat history
The query alone has nothing to search on. A standalone rewrite restores the missing context.
Where does a cross-encoder re-ranker belong in a product-search pipeline?
Before retrieval, to pick the index
After a wide first-stage retrieval, before building the results
Instead of retrieval, over the full catalogue
After the LLM writes its answer
Retrieve many cheap candidates, then re-rank a short list precisely.
Which statements about HyDE are true? Select all that apply.
It embeds a hypothetical answer instead of the question
It can help when questions are short or phrased unlike the documents
It can bias retrieval if the hypothetical answer invents details
It removes the need for a retriever
HyDE changes what is embedded; retrieval still happens, and invented details are its main risk.
The right passage is at rank 23 of 50 candidates and the prompt uses the top 5. Re-ranking moves it to rank 2. What happens to recall@5 for this query?
Rank 23 is outside the top 5; rank 2 is inside. The retriever found it; re-ranking fixed the order.
Search takes 40 ms, the rewrite call 350 ms, and re-ranking costs 20 ms plus 2 ms per candidate. What is the latency with 50 candidates?
“Compare roaming charges in the UAE and the UK” retrieves only UAE documents. What helps most?
Decompose it into one sub-query per country
Multi-part questions need several searches whose results are merged.
Why not run a cross-encoder over all 5 million passages for every query?
Cross-encoders are less accurate than bi-encoders
Nothing can be precomputed, so each query needs 5 million forward passes
They only accept one passage per day
A cross-encoder reads each query–passage pair together, so the cost grows with the corpus for every query.
What are the risks of adding LLM query rewriting? Select all that apply.
The rewrite can drift from what the user meant
It guarantees answers free of hallucination
Rewriting helps recall but costs time and money and can change the meaning. It guarantees nothing about answers.
Multi-query search runs four phrasings and returns four ranked lists. How are they usually merged?
RRF combines rankings robustly without comparing raw scores.
A rewrite call costs ₹0.02 per query and the site serves 3 lakh queries a day. What is the daily cost?
Before indexing, an LLM writes a one-sentence note on where each chunk sits in its document, and the note is embedded with the chunk. What is this called?
Anthropic’s contextual retrieval prepends chunk-specific context before embedding and BM25 indexing.
A pipeline retrieves 5 candidates, re-ranks them and keeps the top 5. Recall did not improve. Why?
Re-ranking can only reorder the same 5 passages; retrieve wider first
The top 5 should be the top 3
To improve recall at 5, the first stage must surface the right passage somewhere in a larger pool.
When is it reasonable to skip LLM query rewriting? Select all that apply.
The query is a precise policy number
The latency budget is tight and the query is already clear
The query is a clear, complete question
The query is a follow-up full of pronouns
Rewrite where it pays: vague and follow-up questions. Clear queries can skip it to save latency.
Your budget is 600 ms. Rewrite plus re-ranking takes 520 ms, and multi-query would add 420 ms. What do you do?
Keep rewrite and re-ranking; skip multi-query or trigger it only for hard queries
940 ms breaks the budget. Add expensive steps only where they are measured to pay off.
What should you log to evaluate query rewriting in production? Select all that apply.
Comparing original, rewrite and retrieved results shows drift and recall problems. The answer alone hides them.
First-stage recall@50 is 0.92. Even with a perfect re-ranker, what is the highest recall@5 you can reach?
A re-ranker cannot surface passages outside the 50 candidates.
Which of these act before retrieval runs? Select all that apply.
Rewriting, HyDE and decomposition shape the search; re-ranking works on its results.
With HyDE, the hypothetical answer mentions the wrong dosage, and retrieval returns a page about a different drug. What went wrong?
The hypothetical answer invented details that steered retrieval
HyDE’s main risk: invented details bias which documents look similar.
You need multilingual re-ranking in production with no GPUs to manage. Which tool fits?
A hosted re-ranking API avoids running models yourself.
What does a cross-encoder take as input and return?
A query–passage pair; a relevance score
It scores pairs directly instead of producing vectors to compare.
qoa: A buyer asks for “2 BHK flats in Pune under 60 lakh”. What max_price_inr should the plan contain?
The planner writes max_price_inr = 60 for “under 60k”. What catches it before any search runs?
A range check such as ge=10,000 in the schema
Validation in code rejects impossible values and sends the error back to the model.
Which of these should a query optimization agent decide? Select all that apply.
The agent plans the query. The embedding model is fixed when the index is built.
A request needs 2 LLM calls at about 700 ms and 2 searches at about 40 ms. How much latency does the agent add?
An investor asks for “large-cap funds with an expense ratio under 1%”. What should the plan contain?
The whole sentence embedded as one query
Filters category = large cap and expense_ratio < 1.0, with little left for the semantic part
BM25 over the fund names only
Both constraints are structured fields; embeddings would only nudge similarity.
“Laptops launched this year” comes back as year = 2024 when it is 2026. What fixes it?
A tighter year range in the schema
Putting today’s date in the system prompt
The model cannot know the current date. A range check passes 2024, so the date must come from the prompt.
Which practices make agentic retrieval safe? Select all that apply.
A typed plan schema validated in code
Logging every plan with its results
Letting the model write raw SQL that runs directly
Structured, validated plans with capped retries and logs are safe. Unchecked raw SQL is not.
An assistant must choose between HR, IT and finance knowledge bases. Which agent decision is this?
Source selection: routing to the right collection
Choosing which collection or tool to query is source selection.
An agent may try up to 3 plans, each with a 700 ms LLM call and a 40 ms search. What is the worst-case added latency?
Which agent failure is hardest to notice?
A valid filter with a wrong value that still returns plenty of results
Nothing fires for a plausible wrong filter. Only logs and an evaluation set reveal it.
On 300 labelled queries, the agent gets 252 right and the fixed pipeline 219. What are their accuracies?
252 ÷ 300 = 0.84 and 219 ÷ 300 = 0.73, a gain of 11 percentage points.
Queries are purely semantic, with no filters, and the latency budget is 150 ms. What do you choose?
A fixed pipeline, because an LLM call would break the budget
With no structured constraints and a tight budget, planning adds cost with no benefit.
What belongs in the agent’s description of each collection? Select all that apply.
Allowed values, such as practice areas
The agent needs fields, values and contents to plan well. Vectors are useless to it.
Which LangChain component turns a request into a query plus metadata filters?
SelfQueryRetriever asks an LLM for a semantic query and structured filters for the vector store.
What does the Weaviate Query Agent do?
Turns natural-language questions into filtered searches across collections
It chooses collections, filters and search methods from a plain-language question, on Weaviate Cloud.
A plan filters department = “Cardio”, but the stored value is “Cardiology”. Which measures prevent this kind of error? Select all that apply.
List allowed values in the schema, for example as an enum
Validate values in code before searching
Log plans and review filters that return few results
Constrained values, validation and logs catch wrong values. A larger k cannot fix a filter that matches nothing.
Re-plan once with feedback when results are too few, then fall back
Always drop every filter on retry
One capped retry with feedback recovers weak searches without runaway cost.
What does adding a query optimization agent cost? Select all that apply.
More cost when retries run, unless they are capped
A larger vector index on disk
The agent adds LLM calls. The index itself is unchanged.
A handler asks for “claims above INR 2 lakh”. What value should the amount filter use?
The plan asks for k = 500, but the schema allows at most 50. What should happen?
Validation fails, and the model is asked again or k is clamped to 50
The schema is the contract: invalid plans are rejected or corrected before any search.
graphrag: What does GraphRAG build before any question arrives?
A graph of entities and relationships with community summaries
What is the SLA for ticket 4471?
What are the main causes of complaints this quarter?
Which garages are linked to claimants who share an agent?
What is the most expensive part of GraphRAG indexing?
One LLM call per chunk, often more.
Which algorithm groups entities into communities in Microsoft GraphRAG?
Which are drawbacks of GraphRAG? Select all that apply.
It cannot answer any fact questions
It can answer facts, but vector RAG is cheaper.
70% at ₹600 and 30% at ₹3,000 per 1,000 queries. Blended cost before routing overhead?
Why route fact questions to vector RAG?
It is cheaper and just as good for them
What does global search do with community summaries?
Maps over them and reduces partial answers
Quality rises from 59% to 82%. Gain in points?
What do lazy variants such as LazyGraphRAG change?
Defer summarisation to query time to cut indexing cost
Use no LLM at all at any point
Before indexing 50 lakh documents, you should?
Index a sample and inspect extraction quality
Which settings shape a GraphRAG index? Select all that apply.
How is GraphRAG different from Graph Memory in module 9?
GraphRAG indexes a document corpus; Graph Memory tracks what an agent learns about users over time
Indexing costs ₹18,000 once and saves 20 analyst hours a month at ₹900 an hour. Months to pay back?
A corpus changes hourly and has no budget for re-indexing. Best choice?
Vector RAG, perhaps with a lighter incremental graph
Then gathers neighbours and source text.
Which outputs does Microsoft GraphRAG indexing produce? Select all that apply.
With 60% theme questions, which mode is most important?
GraphRAG and vector RAG on the same questions, with cost
Quality and cost side by side.

parse.q: Explain why parsing is often the weakest link in a RAG pipeline, and what you would check first.
pts: measure per page or per question
parse.model: Everything downstream works on the text that parsing produced; a scanned page with no OCR or a flattened table simply cannot be retrieved, and no model fixes that. First check how many pages produced little or no text, whether tables kept their headers and whether multi-column pages read in order. Then trace failed questions back to their source page.

parse.q: OCR takes 1.5 seconds a page and 500 of 2,000 pages are scans. How long does OCR add, and how would you cut it?
pts: only OCR pages without a text layer
parse.model: 500 × 1.5 s = 750 s, about 12.5 minutes. OCR only the pages without a text layer rather than every page, run OCR in parallel workers, and re-parse only documents that changed.

parse.q: Answers about loan interest rates are often wrong although the rate tables are in the index. Diagnose.
pts: keep tables as Markdown or HTML
parse.model: The tables were probably flattened into a stream of numbers, so “12.0%” no longer sits next to “24 months”. Extract tables as Markdown or HTML rows with their headers, chunk them without splitting rows, and add table questions to the evaluation set.

chunk.q: How would you choose a chunking strategy for a new corpus of policy documents?
pts: size in a few hundred tokens
chunk.model: Start from the document’s structure: split by section and clause, then recursively to a few hundred tokens with a little overlap. Prepend the title and section path to each chunk. If rules and exceptions span several chunks, search small chunks and return the parent clause. Choose by measuring recall and tokens per answer on real questions, since every change means re-embedding.

chunk.q: A 1.2-million-token corpus is chunked at 400 tokens with 15% overlap. About how many chunks is that, and how many tokens reach the prompt with k = 5?
chunk.model: 1,200,000 ÷ 400 = 3,000 chunks, times 1.15 for overlap ≈ 3,450. Five chunks of 400 tokens send 2,000 tokens to the prompt.

chunk.q: Users say answers miss conditions such as “except after 36 months”. What is happening and how do you fix it?
pts: chunks too small or boundaries wrong
keep clauses whole or return the parent
chunk.model: The rule and its exception landed in different chunks, so only half the clause was retrieved. Split by clause rather than fixed size, add overlap, and use small-to-big retrieval so the whole clause reaches the prompt.

rerank.q: Explain how a cross-encoder re-ranker differs from the retriever, and where it fits.
rerank.model: The retriever embeds the query and each document separately and compares vectors, which is fast enough for millions of items but imprecise. A cross-encoder reads the query and one passage together and outputs a relevance score, which is far more precise but too slow for the whole corpus. So retrieve a wide pool, re-rank it and keep the best few.

rerank.q: Re-ranking costs 2.5 ms a candidate and search takes 40 ms. With a 500 ms budget and 150 ms reserved for everything else, how many candidates can you score?
rerank.model: 500 − 150 − 40 = 310 ms for re-ranking; 310 ÷ 2.5 = 124 candidates. In practice choose 100 and check p95, not just the average.

rerank.q: After adding a re-ranker, English questions improved but Hinglish ones got worse. Why, and what do you change?
rerank.model: The re-ranker was trained on English and scores code-mixed queries poorly, pushing good Hinglish matches down. Use a multilingual re-ranker such as bge-reranker-v2-m3 or Cohere’s multilingual model, and report recall separately for Hinglish.

cite.q: What makes an answer “grounded”, and how would you enforce it in code?
cite.model: Every claim in a grounded answer is supported by a retrieved source. In code: pass sources as documents with citations enabled, check that each cited span is in the source it names, drop sentences without valid support, and reply “not found” when nothing remains. Filter superseded versions before retrieval.

cite.q: Of 80 answers, 7 contained an unsupported claim before verification. Verification removes 80% of them. How many remain, and what rate is that?
cite.model: 7 × 20% = 1.4, so about 1 answer in 80 still has an unsupported claim, roughly 1.75%.

cite.q: Every answer has valid citations, yet staff report advice that is out of date. Explain.
pts: citation is valid but source is stale
cite.model: The citations point to real text in real documents, so verification passes, but the documents are superseded versions still in the index. Mark versions with effective dates, filter to current versions before retrieval, and show the effective date with each source.

llm.q: A chat assistant retrieves nothing useful for follow-up questions. How would you fix it?
pts: check the rewrite does not drift
llm.model: Follow-ups such as “and the other one?” have nothing to search on. Before retrieval, have an LLM rewrite the question into a standalone query using the conversation history, then search with that. Log the rewrites and evaluate them, because a rewrite can drift from what the user meant.

llm.q: Where does a cross-encoder re-ranker belong, and why not use it for everything?
pts: too slow for the whole corpus
llm.model: After a cheap, wide first stage such as hybrid search for the top 50, and before building the prompt. A cross-encoder reads the query and passage together, which is more accurate than comparing two independent vectors, but it can’t precompute anything, so running it over millions of documents per query is far too slow.

llm.q: Your team wants HyDE, multi-query and re-ranking all at once. How do you decide?
pts: add one step at a time
llm.model: Add them one at a time and measure each on a labelled query set: recall@5 or answer quality gained, against the latency and cost added. Keep only the steps that pay for themselves within the latency budget. HyDE in particular can hurt when the hypothetical answer invents details.

qoa.q: In your own words: what does a query optimization agent do before the database is searched?
pts: rewrites the query or chooses source and mode
outputs a plan that code validates
grades results and retries a limited number of times
qoa.model: It reads the natural-language request and produces a structured plan: a short semantic query, exact filters such as price, date and category, the collection to search, the retrieval mode and top-k. Code validates the plan against a typed schema before anything runs. After the search, the agent checks the results, for example whether enough came back, and re-plans once with feedback if they look weak.

qoa.q: The agent’s plans look reasonable, but some answers are quietly wrong. How do you find and prevent silent wrong filters?
pts: evaluate against a labelled set or a fixed pipeline
give context such as today’s date or allowed values
qoa.model: A wrong but valid filter returns plausible results, so no error fires. Log every request with its plan and results, and run the agent on a labelled evaluation set, comparing with a fixed pipeline. Prevent the common causes: give the model today’s date and the allowed values for each field, validate ranges and enumerations in code, and review the logs for filters that exclude most of the collection.

qoa.q: When is a fixed retrieval pipeline better than an agent?
qoa.model: When queries carry no structured constraints, when there is only one collection, or when the latency budget cannot absorb an LLM call of several hundred milliseconds, a fixed pipeline is cheaper and faster. It is also deterministic and easier to test. Add an agent only when an evaluation set shows that planning, such as extracting filters or choosing sources, improves results by enough to justify the extra latency and cost.

graphrag.q: Explain GraphRAG and when you would use it.
graphrag.model: GraphRAG uses an LLM to extract entities and relationships, clusters them into communities and summarises each. Local search answers multi-hop questions from entity neighbours; global search combines community summaries for whole-corpus questions. Indexing is costly, so route only those question types to it.

graphrag.q: 70% local at ₹600 per 1,000, 30% global at ₹3,000, router ₹50. Cost per 1,000 queries?
The indexing quote for 50 lakh documents is too high. What would you try?
graphrag.model: Index a sample and check extraction quality, consider a lazy variant or a lighter graph index, graph only the documents that serve multi-hop or theme questions, and measure quality against vector RAG before scaling.

cases.title: The assistant that quotes the wrong exit load
cases.brief: Dhan Mitra, a mutual-fund distributor, runs a RAG assistant for its relationship managers, answering questions about schemes from scheme information documents, fact sheets and addenda. Compliance has paused it after several wrong answers about charges. The latency budget is two seconds, and you are asked for a plan to fix the pipeline before it goes back live.
evidence: About 30% of the source PDFs are scanned addenda. The index holds almost no text from them, and nobody noticed because ingestion reported success.
Documents are cut into fixed 1,000-token chunks. Several wrong answers quoted an exit load and missed the exception that follows it in the same clause.
In 200 reviewed failures, the right passage was in the retrieved top 50 in 88% of cases, but ranked below tenth in most of them.
Compliance requires a source for every figure shown. Older versions of several documents are still in the index alongside the current ones.
18% of questions are follow-ups such as “and for the direct plan?”, and about 5% mention a date.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.parse: Start here. Thirty per cent of the corpus is in the index as near-empty text, and silently - the ingestion step reported success. Nothing downstream can retrieve, rank or cite a document whose text was never extracted, so every other measurement you take today is taken over 70% of the corpus. Use a parser that handles scans and tables, and add an ingestion check that fails loudly when a page yields almost no text.
why.chunk: Quoting an exit load and missing the exception in the same clause is the chunking pitfall exactly: a fixed 1,000-token cut separates a rule from its qualifier, and the retrieved piece no longer holds the whole answer. Chunk on the document's structure - clause and sub-clause - so a rule and its exception travel together. Do it in the same pass as the parse fix, because both force a full re-embed.
why.rerank: 88% of the right passages are already in the top 50 and most of them sit below tenth, which is the textbook case for a cross-encoder: the pool is right and the order is wrong. Two seconds is ample for re-ranking fifty candidates. Tune the threshold on your own data so the pipeline can say “not found” rather than present the eleventh-best passage as an answer.
why.cite: Compliance requires a source for every figure, and superseded documents sitting in the index make that worse rather than better - a citation can point at a real passage from last year's addendum and look perfectly valid. Attach sources per figure, verify the cited passage actually supports the sentence, and make document version a first-class field so the current one wins.
why.llm: Useful for the 18% of follow-ups: “and for the direct plan?” has no retrievable content on its own and needs rewriting against the conversation. Keep it modest - each rewrite costs latency inside a two-second budget, and a rewrite that drifts from the question is a new failure mode.
why.qoa: Not needed yet: only about 5% of questions carry a date filter, and an agentic retrieval loop would add model calls before every answer to serve one question in twenty. Revisit once the four fixes above are in and you can see what still fails.
why.graphrag: Not needed: every question here is a specific lookup about one scheme's charges, not a whole-corpus question about themes or trends. Indexing a graph would be a large bill for questions nobody is asking.

firstWhy.chunk: The right second step, and the one that explains the headline failure - a rule separated from its exception is how a wrong exit load gets quoted confidently. But re-chunking a corpus whose scanned third contains no text just produces better-shaped empty chunks, and both changes force the same full re-embed, so they belong together with parsing decided first.
firstWhy.rerank: The most efficient-looking fix on the page: the right passage is already in the pool 88% of the time, so reordering fifty candidates is cheap and effective. The catch is in the technique's own pitfall - re-ranking cannot rescue a passage the first stage never retrieved, and 30% of this corpus is not retrievable at all.
firstWhy.cite: Compliance has paused the assistant and this is what compliance asked for, so the pressure is real. But citations over a corpus that still holds superseded versions and is missing a third of its text would be accurate pointers to the wrong document - you would be certifying a pipeline you have not fixed.

cases.model: Start with parsing, because 30% of the corpus is effectively absent and the ingestion step reported success, so every metric measured today is measured over the other 70%: adopt a parser that handles scans and tables, and add a check that fails loudly when a page yields almost no text. Re-chunk on document structure in the same pass, so an exit load and the exception in its clause stay in one retrievable piece - both changes force a full re-embed, so pay it once. Then add a cross-encoder re-ranker, which is the exactly-right tool when 88% of correct passages are already in the top 50 but ranked below tenth, and tune its threshold on your own data so the pipeline can refuse rather than offer the eleventh-best passage. Next make citations real: a source per figure, a check that the cited passage supports the sentence, and document version as an indexed field so superseded addenda stop winning. Finally rewrite conversational follow-ups for the 18% that need it, keeping the added latency inside the two-second budget. An agentic retrieval loop for the 5% with dates can wait, and GraphRAG answers whole-corpus questions nobody here is asking.
cases.note: Three of these five are downstream of the first: re-ranking, citing and rewriting all operate on text that was never extracted for a third of the corpus. Case 2's pipeline is fed clean text and fails at the step before retrieval; Case 3's fails at the step after it.

parse: Symptom 1: 30% of the source PDFs are scans, the index holds almost no text from them, and the ingestion step said it succeeded. Before any question of ranking or chunking - what happened at the very start of this pipeline?
The stage that turns a document into text, and whether tables, columns and scanned pages survived it. The dangerous part of this symptom is the word silently.
Document Parsing and OCR. The first pitfall - scanned pages ingested as blank text, silently - is this symptom exactly.
chunk: Symptom 2: an answer quoted an exit load and missed the exception that follows it in the same clause. The passage was retrieved; it just did not contain the whole truth. What decides that?

How the document was cut up. There is a specific trade-off here between pieces too small to hold a rule and its qualifier, and pieces too large to embed sharply - and a cost to changing your mind later.
Chunking Strategies. Read the pitfall about tiny chunks separating a rule from its exception, and the note that re-chunking means re-embedding everything.
rerank: Symptom 3 is unusually precise: the right passage was in the top 50 in 88% of failures, and below tenth in most of them. The retrieval is finding it. What is going wrong?
The pool is right and the order is wrong, so you need a second, more expensive scorer over a small candidate set - and something that lets the pipeline decline rather than serve its eleventh choice.
Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders. Note the pitfall that it cannot rescue a passage the first stage never retrieved, which is why it is not your first move here.
cite: Symptom 4 has two halves: compliance wants a source for every figure, and older versions of documents are still in the index beside the current ones. What goes wrong when you add citations to a corpus like that?

Tracing each sentence to a source is the goal - but a pointer can be real, resolvable and still wrong, either because the passage does not say what the sentence claims or because it is last year's version.
Citations and Grounded Answers. All three pitfalls apply: a citation that does not support the claim, a valid citation to an outdated policy, and forcing an answer when sources are empty.

drop.qoa: Agentic and corrective RAG earns its model calls when questions carry implicit filters or a first search often misses. What fraction of these questions mention a date - and what would a retrieval loop cost on every other question?
drop.graphrag: GraphRAG answers questions about the whole corpus - themes, trends, multi-hop joins. What kind of question is “what is the exit load on this scheme?”

cases.firstHint: Your set is right, and three of your five choices are measurements or improvements over retrieved text. Ask what fraction of this corpus has any retrievable text at all before deciding which of them to do first.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Compliance has paused the assistant and demands a source for every figure, so the compliance requirement sets the order.
A third of the corpus has no extractable text, so ranking, citing and rewriting are all being measured and improved over the other two thirds.
The wrong exit load answers came from chunks that split a rule from its exception, which is the specific failure that caused the pause.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the rest of the pipeline is standing on. The chunking fault produced the visible incident and the compliance demand is why this is urgent - but a passage that was never extracted cannot be chunked, ranked, cited or rewritten, and the 88% figure that makes re-ranking look so attractive was computed over a corpus missing a third of its text. Fix the input, then measure again.

cases.title: The compliance assistant that answers from last year's circular
cases.brief: A telecom operator's compliance team asks an assistant about obligations drawn from five collections: regulator circulars, licence conditions, internal SOPs, outside legal opinions and board minutes. Everything is born-digital text that parses cleanly. The failures are not about reading the documents - they are about which documents get searched, and whether the answer admits what it is based on.
evidence: 44% of questions carry implicit filters - circular year, licence service area, effective date - and the pipeline searches everything and answers from whichever chunk ranks highest, often a superseded circular.

Which of the five collections gets searched is decided by a keyword rule in the application. It picks wrongly about one time in four, and when it does the answer is drawn confidently from the wrong body of material.
23% of questions are conversational follow-ups such as “and for the Delhi circle?”, which retrieve nothing. Several others are multi-part and need more than one search to answer at all.
Answers quote no source. The team has traced several to superseded circulars still in the index, and the assistant has never once said it could not find an answer.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.qoa: Start here, because symptoms 1 and 2 are the same gap: nothing in this pipeline decides where and under what conditions to search. Let the model plan the retrieval - extract the year, circle and effective date as real filters, choose the collection deliberately rather than by keyword rule, check whether what came back actually answers the question, and retry with different filters when it does not. Cap the retries, and watch the named risk: a wrong filter silently excludes the right results, which is worse than a wrong ranking.
why.llm: 23% of questions have no retrievable content on their own - “and for the Delhi circle?” is meaningless to a search engine - and others need decomposing into several searches. Rewriting against the conversation fixes the first and splitting the question fixes the second. It also feeds the step above: a rewritten, self-contained question is what the planner extracts filters from.
why.cite: An assistant that quotes no source, draws on superseded circulars and has never once said “not found” is asking a compliance team to take its word. Cite per claim, verify that the cited passage supports it, make document version and effective date indexed fields so the current circular wins, and allow a refusal when the sources do not carry the answer.
why.rerank: Useful once the right collection is being searched with the right filters: a cross-encoder puts the best of the narrowed pool on top and gives you a tunable threshold for refusing. Secondary because re-ranking a pool drawn from the wrong collection just promotes the best wrong passage.
why.chunk: Useful: circulars and licence conditions are heavily structured, so chunking on clause boundaries would keep obligations with their provisos. Worth doing, but no symptom here reports a rule separated from its exception - this pipeline's faults sit either side of retrieval, not inside the chunk.
why.parse: Not needed: the brief says the corpus is born-digital and parses cleanly. This is the same module as Case 1, where parsing was the first move - the difference is one fact about the corpus, and it is worth checking that fact before assuming either answer.
why.graphrag: Not needed: these are targeted lookups about specific obligations, not whole-corpus questions about themes. Sending them to a global graph search would pay map-reduce costs for facts a filtered query answers directly.

firstWhy.llm: Very close, and the two are nearly one system - a rewritten question is what the planner reads. But rewriting a follow-up into a self-contained question still leaves it searching all five collections with no date filter, so you would have improved the input to a step that does not exist yet.
firstWhy.cite: This is what a compliance team will demand first and it is unarguably needed. But citations describe where an answer came from, and today that is often the wrong collection and a superseded circular - you would be faithfully documenting the wrong source. Make the retrieval deliberate, then make it accountable.
firstWhy.rerank: Reasonable and cheap, and you will add it. But a cross-encoder reorders the candidates it is given, and one time in four those candidates come from the wrong collection entirely - the best passage in the wrong corpus is still the wrong answer.

cases.model: Start with agentic, corrective retrieval, because the two largest symptoms are both about retrieval being undirected: 44% of questions carry a year, circle or effective date that nothing turns into a filter, and the choice between five collections is made by a keyword rule that is wrong a quarter of the time. Let the model plan the search - extract the filters, choose the collection explicitly, judge whether what came back answers the question, and retry with different filters when it does not - with a hard cap on retries and attention to the fact that a wrong filter excludes silently. Pair it with query rewriting, since 23% of questions are follow-ups with no standalone meaning and others need splitting into several searches; a self-contained question is also what the planner extracts its filters from. Then make answers accountable: cite per claim, verify the cited passage supports it, index version and effective date so superseded circulars lose, and permit an explicit “not found”. Add a cross-encoder to order the narrowed pool and give you a refusal threshold. The corpus parses cleanly, so parsing has nothing to fix, and these are targeted lookups rather than whole-corpus questions.
cases.note: Same module, same kind of complaint, and parsing went from the first move in Case 1 to nothing to do here - on the strength of one sentence about the corpus. The question to ask first is always which stage of the pipeline the evidence actually implicates.

qoa: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together. 44% of questions carry a year, a circle or an effective date that nothing acts on, and which of five collections gets searched is decided by a keyword rule that is wrong a quarter of the time. Who or what is deciding how to search?

Nothing is - and that is the gap. Let the retrieval itself be planned and checked: conditions pulled out as filters, the source chosen on purpose, the result judged, and another attempt made when it does not answer the question.
Agentic and Corrective RAG. Read the pitfall about a wrong filter silently excluding the right results, and the one about capping retries.
llm: Symptom 3: “and for the Delhi circle?” retrieves nothing, and other questions need more than one search to answer. What has to happen to the question before it reaches the index?
Turn what the user typed into something a search engine can actually use - resolved against the conversation, and split when it contains more than one question.
Query Rewriting and HyDE. Note the pitfalls about added latency and about rewrites drifting from what the user meant.
cite: Symptom 4: no sources at all, answers traced to superseded circulars, and an assistant that has never admitted it could not find something. What does a compliance team need from every sentence?
Traceability to a source - plus two harder things: that the source says what the sentence claims, and that it is the version in force.
Citations and Grounded Answers. All three pitfalls are here: unsupported citations, valid citations to outdated policy, and forcing an answer when the sources are empty.

drop.parse: Parsing and OCR fix text that never survived ingestion. What does the brief say about this corpus - and what does that tell you about comparing this case with Case 1?
drop.graphrag: GraphRAG is for whole-corpus questions and multi-hop joins. Is “what does the current circular require in the Delhi circle?” a theme across the corpus, or one filtered lookup?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right and two of them are closely coupled. Ask which one the other is an input to: one of your steps needs a self-contained question, and the other produces one - but only one of them decides which collection gets searched at all.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Nothing decides which collection to search or which filters apply, so 44% of questions and a quarter of all routing are undirected.
23% of questions retrieve nothing at all, which is the largest group of outright failures.
A compliance team is acting on answers that carry no source and are sometimes drawn from superseded circulars.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the others operate on. Rewriting produces a better question and citation documents where the answer came from - but both are inputs and outputs of a retrieval step that currently searches the wrong body of material one time in four, with no filters. Make the search deliberate first; then a rewritten question has somewhere good to go, and a citation points at something worth citing.

cases.title: The review that cannot say what the main issues are
cases.brief: A bank's conduct team holds 480,000 complaint files, ombudsman decisions and internal investigation notes, all born-digital exports from the CRM. Executives do not ask about one complaint - they ask what is going wrong across all of them, and they act on the answers in board papers. A GraphRAG pilot was built and quietly abandoned.
evidence: The questions that matter are whole-corpus: “what are the main drivers of complaints in the Pune region this year”. Passage retrieval returns ten complaints and the assistant generalises from those ten.
Multi-hop questions - “which branches appear in complaints later escalated by the same relationship manager” - need facts joined across documents, and single-passage retrieval returns nothing useful.
Files are cut into fixed 1,200-token chunks, which routinely separate the complaint from its resolution and from its later reclassification, so any theme is assembled from half-records.
Executives act on these summaries in board papers. Asked which complaints a particular claim came from, the assistant cannot say.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.chunk: Start here, and it is the least obvious first move in this module. A 1,200-token cut that separates a complaint from its resolution and its reclassification means every record in this corpus is half a record - and the graph you are about to build extracts its entities and relations from exactly these chunks. Chunk on the record's structure, one complaint with its outcome, before anything reads them.
why.graphrag: This is the right answer to symptoms 1 and 2, and the reason the pilot failed is instructive. Whole-corpus questions about drivers and themes, and multi-hop joins across documents, are what a graph plus community summaries are for; generalising from ten retrieved passages is not an answer to “what are the main drivers”, it is a sample of ten. Check extraction quality on a sample before indexing 480,000 files, route simple factual lookups to ordinary retrieval rather than paying map-reduce for them, and plan incremental updates so the graph does not go stale as complaints are reclassified.
why.cite: Executives are putting these summaries in board papers and the assistant cannot say which complaints a claim rests on. For a synthesised, whole-corpus claim, traceability is harder and matters more: carry the supporting complaint IDs through the summarisation so any assertion can be opened up, and make reclassification visible so a claim is not supported by a complaint whose category has since changed.
why.qoa: Useful: “in the Pune region this year” is an implicit filter on region and date, and deciding deliberately between a graph search and a passage lookup is exactly the routing decision agentic retrieval makes. Worth adding once the graph exists, since it is what keeps simple questions off the expensive path.
why.rerank: Useful for the ordinary factual lookups that remain, where the top few passages decide the answer. It does nothing for whole-corpus synthesis, which is most of what this team asks.
why.parse: Not needed: the files are born-digital CRM exports. Worth stating because it is the opposite of Case 1, where a third of the corpus was unreadable scans - the same module, and the first move changes entirely.
why.llm: Not needed on this evidence: executives ask self-contained analytical questions rather than conversational follow-ups, and nothing here reports a question that retrieved nothing because it lacked context. A rewrite step would add latency to every question to fix a symptom nobody has.

firstWhy.graphrag: The correct diagnosis of this case and the technique the whole module builds to, so wanting it first is the natural reading. But a graph is extracted from chunks, and today a chunk holds a complaint without its resolution - so the entities and relations would be drawn from half-records, which is how the pilot got one in nine entities wrong. Its own pitfall says to check extraction quality before indexing; the chunking is what that quality depends on.
firstWhy.cite: Executives are acting on these summaries in board papers, so traceability is genuinely urgent. But a citation leads back to a chunk, and a chunk currently holds a complaint without its outcome or its reclassification - you would be giving a board paper a reliable pointer to half the record.
firstWhy.qoa: Right that “Pune this year” is a filter and that simple lookups should not go to global search. But routing decides which index answers a question, and the index that should answer most of these questions does not exist yet.

cases.model: Start by re-chunking on the record's own structure, so a complaint travels with its resolution and its reclassification: at 1,200 fixed tokens every record in this corpus is a fragment, and the graph you are about to build extracts its entities and relations from exactly these pieces. Then build GraphRAG, which is what symptoms 1 and 2 actually require - whole-corpus questions about drivers and themes, and multi-hop joins across documents, are not answerable by generalising from ten retrieved passages. Check extraction quality on a sample before indexing all 480,000 files, keep simple factual lookups on ordinary retrieval instead of paying map-reduce for them, and build incremental updates in from the start, since complaints get reclassified and a stale graph is a confidently wrong one. Next make synthesised claims traceable: carry supporting complaint IDs through summarisation so an executive can open any assertion in a board paper, and surface reclassification so a claim is not resting on a category that has since changed. Add agentic routing to choose between graph and passage retrieval and to apply region and date filters, and keep a re-ranker for the factual lookups. The corpus is born-digital, so parsing has nothing to fix, and these are self-contained analytical questions rather than conversational follow-ups.
cases.note: GraphRAG is the right answer here and it is still not the first move, because a graph is only as good as the chunks it was extracted from - which is its own documented pitfall, read one step earlier. Across the three cases the first move was always the stage furthest upstream that the evidence implicated: the parser, the retrieval planner, the chunker.

chunk: Symptom 3: files are cut at 1,200 fixed tokens, which separates a complaint from its resolution and from its later reclassification. Now look at symptoms 1 and 2 and ask what they would be built from.

Whatever reads this corpus - a retriever, a summariser, an entity extractor - reads these pieces. If a piece is half a record, everything downstream inherits that. The question is what the natural unit of this corpus is.
Chunking Strategies. Read the pitfall about separating a rule from its exception and translate it to a complaint and its outcome - and note the cost of changing your mind later.
graphrag: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together: “what are the main drivers of complaints in Pune this year” answered by generalising from ten retrieved passages, and “which branches appear in complaints escalated by the same manager” returning nothing. What do both questions need that passage retrieval structurally cannot give?

One needs the whole corpus rather than a sample of it; the other needs facts from different documents joined together. There is one technique for both - and the brief mentions an abandoned pilot, so read its pitfalls as a post-mortem.

GraphRAG. All three pitfalls explain the failed pilot: indexing before checking extraction on a sample, sending every question to global search, and letting the graph go stale with no incremental update.
cite: Symptom 4: executives put these summaries into board papers, and the assistant cannot say which complaints a claim came from. What is harder about citing a claim that was synthesised across thousands of documents?
The supporting identifiers have to survive the summarisation rather than being discarded by it - and you have to know whether the record they point at still says what it said.
Citations and Grounded Answers. Note the pitfall about a valid citation to an outdated version, and read it alongside the fact that complaints here get reclassified.

drop.parse: Parsing fixes text that did not survive ingestion. What does the brief say these files are - and what does that tell you about why Case 1 began with this and this case does not?
drop.llm: Query rewriting resolves follow-ups like “and the other one?” and splits multi-part questions. Which symptom here describes a question that failed for lack of conversational context?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right, and the famous one is not first. Ask what the graph is built from: its own guidance says to check extraction quality before indexing, and extraction runs over the pieces your other choice defines.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Whole-corpus and multi-hop questions are what the team actually asks, and passage retrieval cannot answer either.
Executives are acting on untraceable summaries in board papers, which is the highest-consequence failure here.
Every record is currently a fragment, and the graph, the summaries and the citations are all built from those fragments.
whyFirst.why: Order by what everything downstream reads. The whole-corpus questions are the point of the project and the board papers are the risk - but the graph extracts its entities from chunks, the summaries are assembled from chunks, and a citation resolves to a chunk. While a chunk holds a complaint without its resolution, each of those inherits a half-record, which is exactly how the pilot produced wrong entities.

parse.t: 500 of 2,000 pages are scans. OCR takes 1.5 seconds a page on one worker. With 5 workers in parallel, how many minutes does OCR take?
parse.a: 500 × 1.5 s = 750 s of OCR work; across 5 workers that is 150 s, or 2.5 minutes. OCR only the pages without a text layer, not all 2,000.
iv: How do you make sure scanned PDFs are actually searchable in a RAG system?

Detect pages without a text layer and OCR them at about 300 dpi with the right languages, such as English and Hindi. Check characters per page after parsing and send near-empty pages to review. Keep page numbers so answers can cite the page, and sample-check OCR quality on real documents.
Why do tables cause so many RAG failures, and what do you do about them?

Naive extraction flattens tables into a stream of numbers, so values lose their row and column headers. Extract tables as Markdown or HTML rows with headers, never split a row across chunks, and add table questions to the evaluation set.
mis: Assuming every PDF has a text layer
Check each page and OCR the ones without text
Flattening tables into plain text
Keep tables as rows with their headers

chunk.t: A corpus of 900,000 tokens is chunked at 300 tokens with no overlap. How many chunks, in thousands?
chunk.a: 900,000 ÷ 300 = 3,000 chunks, or 3 thousand. With 20% overlap it would be about 3,600.
iv: How do you choose chunk size?

Start from the document structure and a few hundred tokens, then measure recall and tokens per answer on real questions. Small chunks match precise facts; larger ones keep conditions together. Small-to-big retrieval gets both: search small, return the parent section.
What is contextual chunking?

Adding context to each chunk before embedding: at minimum the title and section path, or an LLM-written sentence situating the chunk in its document. It helps chunks match questions phrased in the document's own terms, at a one-off ingestion cost.
mis: Picking a chunk size once and never measuring it
Compare strategies on recall and tokens with real questions
Cutting fixed-size chunks through clauses and tables
Split along headings, clauses and rows

rerank.t: Search takes 40 ms and a cross-encoder takes 2.5 ms per candidate. What is the total latency for re-ranking 100 candidates, in milliseconds?
rerank.a: 40 + 100 × 2.5 = 290 ms. Scoring 200 candidates would take 540 ms, over a 500 ms budget.
iv: When is a re-ranker worth adding?
When the right passage is usually retrieved but not in the top few. Measure recall at 50 and recall at 5: a large gap means re-ranking will help; a low recall at 50 means fix retrieval first.
Cross-encoder or LLM re-ranker?

Cross-encoders are fast and precise enough for most pipelines, at a few milliseconds per candidate on a GPU. LLM re-rankers can reason about harder relevance but add hundreds of milliseconds to seconds; use them offline, for small candidate sets, or where latency does not matter.
mis: Re-ranking only the top 5 that will be kept
Score a wide pool, then keep the few
Using an English re-ranker for Hinglish users
Use a multilingual model and report recall per language

cite.t: An assistant answers 80 questions; 9% contain an unsupported claim. Claim-level citations cut that by a fifth, and verification removes 80% of what remains. About how many answers still contain an unsupported claim?
iv: How do you stop a RAG assistant from making things up?

Ground it: answer only from retrieved sources, cite each sentence, verify each citation against its source in code, drop unsupported sentences and abstain when nothing is supported. Measure faithfulness on an eval set and track the abstain rate.
Your citations are all valid but some answers are outdated. Why?

Superseded documents are still in the index, so the model cites real text from old versions. Store version and effective-date metadata, filter to current versions before retrieval and show dates with sources.
mis: Treating a citation as proof
Verify that the cited text is in the source and supports the claim
Leaving old versions in the index
Filter by version metadata before retrieval

llm.t: Retrieval returns 50 candidates and the right passage is at rank 23. Your prompt uses the top 5. After re-ranking it moves to rank 2. What happens to recall@5 for this query?
llm.a: It goes from 0 (rank 23 is outside the top 5) to 1. The retriever had found it; the ranking was the problem, which is exactly what re-ranking fixes.
iv: What is HyDE, and when does it help?

Hypothetical Document Embeddings: an LLM writes a plausible answer and you embed that instead of the question. It helps when questions are short or phrased very differently from the documents, and can hurt if the hypothetical answer invents false details.
Where does a re-ranker go in the pipeline?
After a wide, cheap retrieval step (hybrid top 50–100) and before building the prompt. It improves precision at the very top, which is what the model sees.
mis: Re-ranking only the top 5 you already had
Retrieve wide (50–100), then re-rank
Rewriting every query
Rewrite vague or conversational queries; skip clear ones to save latency

qoa.t: Turn “2 BHK flats in Pune under 60 lakh, ready to move” into a search plan.
qoa.a: query: “2 BHK flat”; filters: city = Pune, bedrooms = 2, price < 6,000,000, status = ready_to_move; mode: hybrid; k: 10–20. Code checks the city against known values and the price as a number before running.
iv: What is self-querying retrieval?

An LLM turns a natural-language request into a semantic query plus structured metadata filters that the database applies exactly. It fixes requests with implicit constraints that pure vector search ignores.
How do you make agentic retrieval safe and debuggable?
Constrain the plan to a typed schema, validate fields and values in code, cap retries, log every plan with its results, and compare against a fixed pipeline on an eval set.
mis: Letting the model write raw SQL or filters unchecked
Use a structured plan validated in code
Unlimited retry loops
Cap retries and fall back to a fixed pipeline

graphrag.t: 70% of questions go to local search at ₹600 per 1,000 and 30% to global at ₹3,000 per 1,000, plus ₹50 per 1,000 for the router. What is the cost per 1,000 queries in ₹?
iv: How does GraphRAG differ from vector RAG?

Vector RAG retrieves chunks similar to the question. GraphRAG first extracts entities and relationships into a graph, clusters it into communities with summaries, and answers multi-hop questions by walking the graph and whole-corpus questions by combining community summaries.
When is GraphRAG not worth it?
When most questions are single-fact lookups that vector RAG already answers, or the corpus changes too fast to re-index affordably.
mis: Sending every question to global search
Route simple facts to vector RAG
Indexing everything before checking extraction
Inspect entities on a sample first

gloss: OCR
Optical character recognition: turning images of text, such as scanned pages, into machine-readable text.
text layer
The embedded, selectable text in a digital PDF; scanned pages have none.
reading order
The sequence in which blocks of a page should be read, which matters for multi-column layouts.
chunk overlap
Tokens repeated at the end of one chunk and the start of the next, so boundary sentences are not lost.
small-to-big retrieval
Searching small chunks for precision, then returning their larger parent section to the model.
contextual chunk header
The document title and section path prepended to a chunk before embedding.
query rewriting
Using a model to turn a vague or conversational question into a standalone search query.
re-ranking
Reordering a retrieved candidate list with a more precise model, keeping only the best few.
grounded answer
An answer whose every claim is supported by the provided sources.
citation verification
Checking in code that each cited span exists in its source and supports the claim.
corrective RAG
A pattern that grades retrieved passages and rewrites the query, switches source or abstains when they are weak.
community summary
An LLM-written report of a cluster of related entities in a GraphRAG index.
global search
GraphRAG query mode that maps over community summaries and reduces them into one answer about the whole corpus.
Leiden algorithm
A community detection method that groups densely connected nodes, used by GraphRAG at several levels.

Chunking by clause at 256 tokens with the section path prepended keeps the rule and exception together, and recall at 5 rises from 67% to 90% while tokens per answer fall from 5,120 to 2,100.

Answer quality rises from 59 to 82 percent at ₹1,370 per 1,000 queries.

Answerable questions rise from 47 with the text layer only, to 68 with OCR, to 89 of 100 with tables and layout.

header.lede: Retrieval-augmented generation is a pipeline, and it fails at its weakest step. Parse documents so scans, tables and columns survive, chunk them so answers stay whole, rewrite vague questions, re-rank so the best passages reach the model, and cite every claim so people can check it.
